claims.claim: UAS-RFP expression resulting from heat shock induced DVE>>GAL4 was observed at 6 hr PHS in the cells surrounding the ablated salm domain, and persisted throughout the recovery period.
claims.source: By comparison, UAS-RFP expression resulting from heat shock induced DVE>>GAL4 was observed at 6 hr PHS (Figure 3H) in the cells surrounding the ablated salm domain, and persisted throughout the recovery period (Figure 3H–K), demonstrating that cells that drive the regenerative growth can be targeted for manipulation using DUAL Control, and that ablation and UAS-driven gene expression can be temporally and spatially separated.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 3H-K.

claims.claim: When ablated in early L3 using DUAL Control with rpr, around 95% of wings produced were in the 'wild type' or 'nicked' category, indicating that regeneration was mostly complete.
claims.source: When ablated in early L3, around 95% of wings produced were in the 'wild type' or 'nicked' category, indicating that regeneration was mostly complete (Figure 3M).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3M.

claims.claim: Ablation in late L3 using DUAL Control with rpr yielded many more 'full notch' or 'ablated' wings, demonstrating the loss of regenerative capacity in wing discs during development.
claims.source: By comparison, ablation in late L3 yielded many more 'full notch' or 'ablated' wings (Figure 3M), demonstrating the loss of regenerative capacity in wing discs during development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3M.

claims.claim: Ablation with egr using DUAL Control resulted in weaker adult phenotypes and lower levels of activated caspase compared to rpr.
claims.source: Ablation with egr resulted in weaker adult phenotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and lower levels of activated caspase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claims.claim: Both Wg and Mmp1 protein are detected following ablation with rpr, and more so with egr due to its stronger activation of the JNK pathway.
claims.source: Both Wg and Mmp1 protein are detected following ablation with rpr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), and more so with egr due to its stronger activation of the JNK pathway (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: Both DRMS enhancers for wg and Mmp1 are activated by DUAL Control ablation.
claims.source: Both genes have experimentally validated DRMS enhancers, which are activated by DUAL Control ablation (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4A-B.

claims.claim: Targeting either wg or Mmp1 for knockdown with RNAi using DUAL Control strongly decreases the damage-induced expression of both proteins.
claims.source: Targeting either wg or Mmp1 for knockdown with RNAi using this system strongly decreases the damage-induced expression of both proteins, while the amount of cell death appears unaffected (Figure 4C–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4C-D.

claims.claim: The extent of regeneration is reduced when wg or Mmp1 are knocked down using DUAL Control.
claims.source: The extent of regeneration, as assessed by the change in adult wing phenotypes in response to ablation with rpr, is reduced in each case (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Mmp1 for the same duration in the absence of ablation yields little to no effect on adult wings.
claims.source: Knockdown of Mmp1 for the same duration in the absence of ablation yields little to no effect on adult wings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), while knockdown of wg without ablation produces patterning defects localized to the distal wing edge (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) that are clearly distinguishable from the wing tissue loss that follows ablation.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claims.claim: wg is required for both regrowth following damage and repatterning.
claims.source: Thus, wg is required for both regrowth following damage and repatterning.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Myc using RNAi directed to regenerating tissue with DUAL Control following ablation with rpr showed a dramatic reduction in regeneration.
claims.source: Knockdown of Myc using RNAi directed to regenerating tissue with either DUAL Control PDM>>GAL4 or DVE>>GAL4 following ablation with rpr showed a dramatic reduction in regeneration (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Myc improves adult wing size and morphology following ablation.
claims.source: Consistently, overexpression of Myc improves adult wing size and morphology (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The phenotypes resulting from Myc manipulation likely result from changes in damage-induced proliferation.
claims.source: An E2F reporter (PCNA-GFP) shows that these phenotypes likely result from changes in damage-induced proliferation in response to altered levels of Myc (Figure 4G–J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 4G-J.

claims.claim: Knockdown of upd1 or upd2 appears to strongly reduce regeneration.
claims.source: Knockdown of the JAK/STAT upd1 or upd2 appears to strongly reduce regeneration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), while knockdown of upd3, which does not have a damage-responsive peak, also mildly reduces regeneration but the effect is less significant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Knockdown of the transcription factor Stat92E or receptor domeless (dome) results in less-complete wings, confirming the requirement for JAK/STAT signaling in regenerating tissue.
claims.source: Knockdown of the transcription factor Stat92E or receptor domeless (dome) also results in less-complete wings (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E), confirming the requirement for JAK/STAT signaling in regenerating tissue surrounding the ablation domain.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: CG9572 is predicted to encode a 441 amino acid protein of unknown function.
claims.source: CG9572 is predicted to encode a 441 amino acid protein of unknown function.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a description of the gene.

claims.claim: CG9572 has strong sequence similarity to the EGF domain repeats of the Jagged protein.
claims.source: In order to better characterize CG9572, we performed protein blast (blastp) and alignment scoring, which revealed strong sequence similarity to the EGF domain repeats of the Jagged protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), a membrane-bound ligand for Notch in vertebrates (Lindsell et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Jagged.

claims.claim: The CG9572 peptide sequence is predicted to contain seven EGF-type repeats that each displays a characteristic spacing of cysteine residues.
claims.source: The peptide sequence is predicted to contain seven EGF-type repeats that each displays a characteristic spacing of cysteine residues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: CG9572 has a 14-amino acid hydrophobic stretch close to its N-terminus that is likely to function as a signal peptide.
claims.source: Similar to Jagged, CG9572 also has a 14-amino acid hydrophobic stretch close to its N-terminus that is likely to function as a signal peptide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Unlike Jagged or other Notch ligands, CG9572 lacks a second hydrophobic stretch that would serve as a transmembrane domain, or a Delta/Serrate/LAG-2 (DSL) domain.
claims.source: However, unlike Jagged or other Notch ligands it lacks a second hydrophobic stretch that would serve as a transmembrane domain, or a Delta/Serrate/LAG-2 (DSL) domain characteristic of Notch ligands (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: When UAS-aspr::HA was expressed in the posterior compartment using en-GAL4, HA staining appeared to be cytoplasmic.
claims.source: When a tagged version, UAS-aspr::HA, was expressed in the posterior compartment using en-GAL4, HA staining appeared to be cytoplasmic (Figure 5B), localizing towards the apical surface of the disc proper (Figure 5C) and with punctae observed in the anterior compartment.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5B-C.

claims.claim: When hh-GAL4 driver was used to express aspr::HA, punctae were observed throughout the anterior compartment consistent with the Aspr protein being secreted from cells.
claims.source: When the stronger hh-GAL4 driver was used, punctae were observed throughout the anterior compartment consistent with the Aspr protein being secreted from cells (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Overexpression of aspr in the whole wing pouch using rn-GAL4 does not result in an observable phenotype in the adult wing.
claims.source: Overexpression of aspr in the whole wing pouch using rn-GAL4 does not result in an observable phenotype in the adult wing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), but expression in the posterior compartment infrequently causes abnormal folding in the pouch at the boundary with wild type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and C.

claims.claim: aspr is expressed at low levels in the ventral and lateral areas of undamaged L3 wing discs.
claims.source: In undamaged L3 wing discs, in situ hybridization shows aspr is expressed at low levels in the ventral and lateral areas of the disc at low levels (Figure 5E–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5E-F.

claims.claim: Upon damage in early L3 discs, aspr is upregulated strongly in the region of the blastema.
claims.source: Upon damage in early L3 discs, aspr is upregulated strongly in the region of the blastema, as shown in discs ablated by both rnts>egr (Figure 5G,M) and DUAL Control ablation with egr (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5G, I, M.

claims.claim: In damaged discs from late L3 larvae, aspr has much weaker damage-induced expression.
claims.source: In damaged discs from late L3 larvae, aspr has much weaker damage-induced expression (Figure 5H,J,N).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5H, J, N.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aspr in the developing wing pouch using rn-GAL4 in undamaged discs has little effect on adult wing size or patterning.
claims.source: Knockdown of aspr with two different RNAi lines in the developing wing pouch using rn-GAL4 in undamaged discs has little effect on adult wing size or patterning (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and data not shown).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aspr in mid L3 discs using en-GAL4 delays the onset of expression of the Notch target cut at the prospective wing margin in the posterior compartment.
claims.source: However, we found that knockdown of aspr in mid L3 discs using en-GAL4 delays the onset of expression of the Notch target cut at the prospective wing margin in the posterior compartment (Figure 5O–Q), suggesting aspr might promote Notch signaling during normal development.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5O-Q.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aspr results in weak reduction in fluorescence of a Notch reporter, NRE-GFP.
claims.source: This is also shown by the weak reduction in fluorescence of a Notch reporter, NRE-GFP (Zacharioudaki and Bray, 2014; Figure 5R–S).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5R-S, with citation to the reporter.

claims.claim: Aspr is a secreted regulator of Notch signaling in the wing, which is strongly activated in regenerating tissue upon damage.
claims.source: These data suggest that Aspr is a secreted regulator of Notch signaling in the wing, which is strongly activated in regenerating tissue upon damage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aspr using DUAL Control reduces the extent of regeneration.
claims.source: To address whether aspr is necessary for regeneration, we used DUAL Control to reduce its expression in regenerating cells in mid-L3 discs using the two different RNAi lines following rpr ablation of the wing pouch. At this stage Cut expression at the margin is beginning to be established (Figure 5R), while ablation at an earlier stage leads to a delay in development and hinders Cut expression. Upon aspr knockdown the presence of Cut in these discs is markedly reduced (Figure 5T–U), suggesting that ablation combined with the loss of aspr may limit Cut expression that has already been initiated. The extent of regeneration is also decreased (Figure 5V).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 5T-U, V.

claims.claim: aspr hemizygous animals (Mi[MIC]CG9572[MI02471]/Y) show a strongly decreased ability to regenerate when ablated with DUAL Control.
claims.source: aspr hemizygous animals have no obvious developmental defects but show a strongly decreased ability to regenerate when ablated with DUAL Control (Figure 5V) and rnts>egr (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5V and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: Expression of Aspr::HA does not strongly affect regeneration.
claims.source: Expression of Aspr::HA does not strongly affect regeneration (Figure 5—figure supplement 2H), indicating that while it is necessary for regeneration, ectopic expression alone it is not sufficient to improve it, as we have demonstrated with other pro-regeneration genes such as wg (Harris et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2H, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The strongest damage-responsive change in chromatin accessibility of all detected DRMS peaks was at the apontic (apt) gene.
claims.source: From our ATAC-seq dataset we noted that the strongest damage-responsive change in chromatin accessibility of all detected DRMS peaks was at the apontic (apt) gene (Figure 2D, Figure 6A and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2D and 6A.

claims.claim: DNA spanning peak 4931 at the apt locus functions as a DRMS enhancer in vivo.
claims.source: We have shown that DNA spanning this peak (Peak 4931) does indeed function as a DRMS enhancer in vivo (Figure 2G–G'), while the data of Khan et al. shows that apt is transcriptionally upregulated in blastema cells (Khan et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2G-G', with citation to Khan et al.

claims.claim: apt encodes a b-Zip transcription factor that has been characterized in tracheal development and formation of both male and female germlines.
claims.source: apt is also known as trachea defective (tdf), and encodes a b-Zip transcription factor that has been characterized in tracheal development (Eulenberg and Schuh, 1997; Gellon et al., 1997) and formation of both male and female germlines (Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Monahan and Starz-Gaiano, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claims.claim: In the male germline, decreasing apt function results in increased expression of JAK/STAT targets, suggesting apt functions to restrict JAK/STAT signaling.
claims.source: In the male germline, decreasing apt function results in increased expression of JAK/STAT targets, suggesting apt functions, at least in this context, to restrict JAK/STAT signaling (Starz-Gaiano et al., 2008; Monahan and Starz-Gaiano, 2016), which is known to be required for wing disc regeneration (Katsuyama et al., 2015; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text with citations to published research.

claims.claim: Apt is expressed at high levels in the squamous cells of the peripodial epithelium and tracheal tubes of undamaged developing wing discs throughout L3.
claims.source: Using an antibody that recognizes the Apt protein (Liu et al., 2003), we found that Apt is expressed at high levels in the squamous cells of the peripodial epithelium and tracheal tubes of undamaged developing wing discs throughout L3, and expression is not obviously above background in cells of the disc proper (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B, with citation to the antibody.

claims.claim: Apt can be detected in the disc proper following damage in early L3, but not in late L3.
claims.source: However, optical section imaging of ablated discs shows that Apt can be detected in the disc proper following damage in early L3 (Figure 6B), but not in late L3 (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6B-C.

claims.claim: Knockdown of apt in regeneration-competent early L3 discs using DUAL Control results in adult wings that are more complete than in ablated controls.
claims.source: To test whether apt is necessary for regeneration, we reduced its expression using DUAL Control by expressing an apt RNAi transgene in regeneration-competent early L3 discs. In view of the demonstration that apt can promote wing growth by promoting Hedgehog expression (Wang et al., 2017), we were surprised to find that the adult wings were more complete than in ablated controls not expressing the apt RNAi (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D, with citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Knockdown of apt in late L3 discs using DUAL Control results in adult wings that are more complete than in controls.
claims.source: We then examined the effect of apt knockdown in late L3 discs and found that, once again, adult wings were more complete than in controls (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: apt normally acts to limit regeneration following damage.
claims.source: These observations indicate that apt knockdown either protects discs from damage during the ablation phase or promotes regeneration. Since the levels of cleaved caspase DCP1 appeared similar in the presence and absence of apt knockdown (Figure 6E–F), this suggests that apt normally acts to limit regeneration following damage.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data shown in Figures 6E-F.

claims.claim: A hypomorphic apt mutant (aptK15608/+) shows a mild increase in regenerative ability compared to wild type at both time points when ablated with DUAL Control and rnts>egr.
claims.source: This is corroborated by a hypomorphic apt mutant (aptK15608/+, [Eulenberg and Schuh, 1997]), which also shows a mild increase in regenerative ability compared to wild type at both time points when ablated with DUAL Control and rnts>egr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D, with citation to the mutant.

claims.claim: With apt knockdown, there is an increase in the activity of a Stat92E reporter specifically in blastema cells.
claims.source: We observed the expression of a fluorescent Stat92E reporter (STAT-GFP) in late L3 discs ablated with DUAL Control in the presence of apt knockdown. Normally at this stage, STAT activity is minimal in regenerating cells of ablated discs (Figure 6E). However, with apt knockdown, we found an increase in the activity of this reporter specifically in blastema cells (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6E-F.

claims.claim: apt might affect regeneration by influencing JAK/STAT activity.
claims.source: As apt is known to act in the germline to limit JAK/STAT signaling, we examined whether it might affect regeneration by influencing JAK/STAT activity.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on known function of apt.

claims.claim: Inhibition of extra sex combs (esc) specifically during the regeneration period consistently improved regeneration, even in discs ablated in early L3.
claims.source: However, inhibition of the Polycomb group gene extra sex combs (esc), which encodes a component of the PRC2 complex (reviewed by Kassis et al., 2017), specifically during the regeneration period consistently improved regeneration, even in discs ablated in early L3 (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6I, with citation to review of PRC2 complex.

claims.claim: Even a small reduction in esc levels is likely to improve regeneration.
claims.source: Under these conditions, we observed no adult wing defects when esc was knocked down in unablated wings for this short duration (data not shown). Thus, even a small reduction in esc levels is likely to improve regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the observation that knockdown doesn't cause developmental defects.

claims.claim: Ablation in a heterozygous esc background (esc5/+) leads to improved regeneration when ablated with rnts>egr.
claims.source: Ablation in a heterozygous esc background (esc5/+) similarly leads to improved regeneration when ablated with rnts>egr (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), although this effect was not significant when ablated using DUAL Control, unlike targeted knockdown with RNAi (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: The level of GFP expression from DRMSWnt, DRMSMmp1, and DRMSaspr reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls.
claims.source: To test whether the improved regenerative capacity of esc knockdown was due to alteration of DRMS activity, we examined the activity of three different DRMS reporters, DRMSWnt, DRMSMmp1, and DRMSaspr, in late L3 discs expressing escRNAi. The level of GFP expression from all of the reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls, as was wg and Mmp1 expression (Figure 6J–K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G), indicating that the loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 6J-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D-G.

claims.claim: The loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
claims.source: The level of GFP expression from all of the reporters was increased in ablated discs with esc knockdown compared to controls, as was wg and Mmp1 expression (Figure 6J–K and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–G), indicating that the loss of esc leads to improved regeneration in part via reactivation of multiple DRMS enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data.

claims.claim: Reducing Polycomb-mediated silencing appears capable of overcoming the suppression of a regeneration program that operates simultaneously at multiple loci in the genome.
claims.source: Thus, reducing Polycomb-mediated silencing appears capable of overcoming the suppression of a regeneration program that operates simultaneously at multiple loci in the genome.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The reduced expression of wg and Wnt6 elicited by damage as discs mature can be explained by the properties of a damage-responsive and maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancer that lies between the two genes.
claims.source: We previously showed that the reduced expression of wg and Wnt6 elicited by damage as discs mature can be explained by the properties of a damage-responsive and maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancer that lies between the two genes (Harris et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work with citation.

claims.claim: Manipulating the DRMSWnt enhancer by deleting the maturity silencing module restores damage-responsive wg expression in mature discs, but this alone is insufficient to preserve regenerative capacity.
claims.source: Manipulating this enhancer by deleting the maturity silencing module restores damage-responsive wg expression in mature discs, but this alone is insufficient to preserve regenerative capacity at this stage of development.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claims.claim: The overall effect of the expression of multiple genes regulated by DRMS enhancers is to promote regeneration.
claims.source: Since the manipulation of a chromatin silencing factor, esc, can de-repress at least three DRMS enhancers, and also promote regeneration, it is likely that the overall effect of the expression of multiple genes regulated by DRMS enhancers is to promote regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: The number of DRMS regions identified using ATAC-seq are likely to be an underestimate since the assay examined chromatin changes using whole discs, in which only a small proportion of cells are undergoing regeneration.
claims.source: However, it is important to note that the number of regions we identified using ATAC-seq are likely to be an underestimate since our assay examined chromatin changes using whole discs, in which only a small proportion of cells are undergoing regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a caveat about the ATAC-seq approach.

claims.claim: Knockdown of aspr adversely impacted regenerative growth but produced no obvious effect on the normal development of the wing except perhaps a delay in the development of the wing margin.
claims.source: Knockdown of aspr adversely impacted regenerative growth but produced no obvious effect on the normal development of the wing except perhaps a delay in the development of the wing margin.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of the aspr knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Following aspr knockdown, expression of the markers at the margin such as Cut and the Notch reporter was delayed both in normal and regenerating discs.
claims.source: We have shown that following aspr knockdown, expression of the markers at the margin such as Cut and the Notch reporter was delayed both in normal and regenerating discs, suggesting that aspr could potentially promote Notch signaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of the aspr knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Aspr has sequence similarity to the vertebrate Notch ligand Jagged.
claims.source: Our analysis reveals that Aspr has sequence similarity to the vertebrate Notch ligand Jagged (Lindsell et al., 1995), raising the possibility that its influence on Notch signaling could be as a ligand.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis with citation.

claims.claim: Unlike most Notch ligands characterized to date, Aspr lacks a DSL domain or a predicted transmembrane domain.
claims.source: However, unlike most Notch ligands characterized to date, Aspr lacks a DSL domain or a predicted transmembrane domain.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Non-canonical Notch ligands that lack a DSL domain have been identified in mammals and have been shown to regulate Notch signaling when engineered into Drosophila.
claims.source: Non-canonical Notch ligands that lack a DSL domain have been identified in mammals (Baladrón et al., 2005; Falix et al., 2012) and have been shown to regulate Notch signaling when engineered into Drosophila (Bray et al., 2008), while several Notch ligands have been characterized in C. elegans that lack transmembrane domains (Chen and Greenwald, 2004; Komatsu et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claims.claim: Being anchored to the membrane is thought to be crucial for the mechanism by which Notch ligands function in Drosophila.
claims.source: Being anchored to the membrane is thought to be crucial for the mechanism by which Notch ligands function in Drosophila; endocytosis of the ligand engaged to Notch is presumed to generate the mechanical force that alters Notch conformation and renders it susceptible to proteolytic cleavage, which eventually results in nuclear translocation of the intracellular domain (Parks et al., 2000; Langridge and Struhl, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claims.claim: It is unlikely that Aspr could function as a canonical Notch ligand based on the view that membrane anchoring is crucial for Notch activation.
claims.source: Thus, at least based on this view of Notch signaling, it is unlikely that Aspr could function as a canonical Notch ligand.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the lack of transmembrane domain and current understanding of Notch signaling.

claims.claim: Notch signaling is thought to function as part of double repressive mechanism that controls regenerative growth.
claims.source: Moreover, Notch signaling is thought to function as part of double repressive mechanism (Herranz et al., 2008) that controls regenerative growth (Smith-Bolton et al., 2009), and is reduced in blastema cells to permit Myc-dependent growth.
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claims.claim: Overexpression of aspr did not appear to increase Notch signaling, at least as assessed by activation of the Notch reporter.
claims.source: Importantly, overexpression of aspr did not appear to increase Notch signaling, at least as assessed by activation of the Notch reporter.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claims.claim: The role of Aspr in promoting regeneration could be independent of a direct influence on Notch signaling.
claims.source: Therefore, the role of Aspr in promoting regeneration could be independent of a direct influence on Notch signaling and remains to be explored further.
claims.evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the observations.

claims.claim: Knockdown of apt appears to improve regeneration in discs ablated in either early or late L3.
claims.source: In addition to aspr, we also found that the transcriptional regulator apt functions in regeneration, although in contrast to aspr, knockdown of apt appears to improve regeneration in discs ablated in either early or late L3.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of the apt knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Knockdown of apt increased expression of a STAT reporter, suggesting this improvement might be via increased JAK/STAT signaling.
claims.source: Knockdown of apt increased expression of a STAT reporter, suggesting this improvement might be via increased JAK/STAT signaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the data.

claims.claim: Reducing JAK/STAT signaling reduced tissue loss following egr-induced ablation, but did not seem to compromise the extent of compensatory proliferation.
claims.source: A previous study has shown that reducing JAK/STAT signaling reduced tissue loss following egr-induced ablation, but did not seem to compromise the extent of compensatory proliferation (La Fortezza et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claims.claim: Overexpression of upd1 or upd2 concurrently with ablation did not improve regeneration.
claims.source: Furthermore, the overexpression of upd1 or upd2 concurrently with ablation did not improve regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work.

claims.claim: Reducing esc activity derepressed at least three DRMS enhancers that were tested using reporter gene constructs.
claims.source: We also found that reducing PcG-mediated repression via knockdown of esc improved overall regeneration. Reducing esc activity derepressed at least three DRMS enhancers that were tested using reporter gene constructs.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of the esc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: It is likely that many DRMS enhancers are regulated by Polycomb-mediated silencing.
claims.source: Since a reduction in esc levels alleviates silencing at multiple DRMS enhancers, it is likely that many of these other enhancers are also regulated by Polycomb-mediated silencing, as for DRMSWnt.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the esc knockdown experiments.

claims.claim: Enhancer accessibility is an important mechanism that regulates various properties of imaginal discs, including specification of their identity during development and cellular proliferation.
claims.source: These findings parallel those of other groups who have used chromatin profiling in imaginal discs to show that enhancer accessibility is an important mechanism that regulates various properties of imaginal discs, including specification of their identity during development and cellular proliferation (McKay and Lieb, 2013; Ma et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is stated with citations to published research.

claims.claim: Distal enhancers for key cell cycle regulators such as cyclin E and string become less accessible as development proceeds, independently of cell-cycle status.
claims.source: In a recent study that investigated the basis of terminal exit from the cell cycle in cells of the Drosophila wing disc (Ma et al., 2019) it was found that distal enhancers for key cell cycle regulators such as cyclin E and string become less accessible as development proceeds. This occurs independently of cell-cycle status but instead seems to be governed by a temporal program.
claims.evidence: This is stated with citation to published research.

claims.claim: The robust exit from the cell-cycle could potentially be explained by reduced levels of many cell-cycle regulators caused by the silencing of enhancers at multiple loci.
claims.source: The robust exit from the cell-cycle could potentially be explained by reduced levels of many cell-cycle regulators caused by the silencing of enhancers at multiple loci.

results.result: Drosophila imaginal discs lose regenerative capacity as they mature from early to late third larval instar (L3). Using DUAL Control ablation, approximately 95% of early L3 discs regenerated completely, while late L3 discs showed significantly reduced regeneration with many more 'full notch' or 'ablated' wings.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12, C58, and C59 collectively demonstrate age-dependent loss of regeneration through both cited prior work and new experimental data using DUAL Control. The quantitative wing scoring data (Figure 3M) provides clear statistical evidence (p<0.0001) of reduced regenerative capacity in late L3 compared to early L3.

results.result: The loss of regenerative capacity coincides with reduced damage-responsive expression of multiple genes including wg, Wnt6, Mmp1, and aspr. These genes show strong upregulation following damage in early L3 discs but much weaker expression in late L3 discs.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C13, C30, C82, and C83 are well-supported by immunofluorescence data (Figures 1F-G, 5G-J) and in situ hybridization showing reduced damage-induced expression of multiple regeneration-associated genes in mature discs. The correlation between reduced gene expression and loss of regenerative capacity is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: A damage-responsive, maturity-silenced (DRMS) enhancer exists at the Mmp1 locus. This enhancer contains separable damage-responsive (Mmp1-A) and maturity-silencing (Mmp1-B) modules, with the silencing dependent on Polycomb-mediated repression.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C23, C26-27, C31-35 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: sequence analysis identifying conserved motifs (Figure 1A-B), GFP reporter assays showing damage-responsive and maturity-silenced activity (Figures 1D-L), functional dissection of enhancer modules, and genetic experiments with Polycomb mutants (Figures 1M-N) demonstrating PcG-dependent silencing.

results.result: ATAC-seq analysis identified 222 damage-responsive regions in early L3 and 33 in late L3, with 28 regions classified as DRMS. The chromatin landscape is more responsive to damage in immature than mature discs, with 729 regions becoming less accessible with maturity in the context of damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-43 are supported by genome-wide ATAC-seq data with appropriate statistical analysis. However, the authors acknowledge limitations (C37) that whole-disc analysis likely underestimates DRMS regions due to signal dilution from non-regenerating cells. The use of relaxed statistical cutoffs (padj<0.1) is justified but introduces some uncertainty. The enrichment analysis (C43, Figure 2—supplement 1F) supports enhancer localization.

results.result: Multiple DRMS enhancers were experimentally validated near genes including wg/Wnt6, Mmp1 (two enhancers), CG9572, ftz-f1, apt, and bru2. All tested enhancers showed damage-responsive expression in early L3 that was reduced in late L3.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C45, C46, and C48 are well-supported by ATAC-seq data (Figure 2A-B) and transgenic GFP reporter assays (Figures 2C-H'). All four candidate regions tested showed the predicted DRMS behavior with no activity in undamaged discs (Figure 2—supplement 2A-D), confirming the utility of the ATAC-seq approach for identifying functional DRMS enhancers.

results.result: DUAL Control is a novel GAL4-independent ablation system that permits simultaneous tissue-specific ablation via LexA and sustained GAL4-driven gene expression in regenerating tissue. The system can be activated with a single 45-minute heat shock and allows temporal separation of ablation and regeneration phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-57 describing DUAL Control are well-supported by detailed characterization including time-course analysis (Figures 3G-K), fluorescent reporter validation (Figures 3C-D, H-K), and optimization experiments (Figure 3—supplement 1A-D). The system successfully addresses limitations of previous GAL4/UAS-based ablation methods by providing independent spatial and temporal control.

results.result: Wg and Mmp1 are required for regeneration. RNAi knockdown of either gene using DUAL Control strongly reduced damage-induced protein expression and significantly impaired regeneration, while knockdown without ablation had minimal or distinguishable effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-66 are supported by immunofluorescence showing reduced protein expression upon RNAi knockdown (Figures 4C-D), quantitative wing scoring demonstrating impaired regeneration (Figure 4E, p<0.0001), and appropriate controls showing minimal developmental effects (Figure 4—supplement 1C-D). The data confirm functional requirements for these DRMS-regulated genes in regeneration.

results.result: Myc is required for regeneration and acts by regulating damage-induced proliferation. Knockdown of Myc dramatically reduced regeneration while overexpression improved it, with effects correlating with changes in E2F reporter activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-69 are supported by wing scoring data showing dramatic effects of Myc manipulation (Figure 4F, p<0.0001) and PCNA-GFP reporter data linking phenotypes to proliferation changes (Figures 4G-J). The bidirectional effects (loss-of-function and gain-of-function) strengthen the conclusion about Myc's role in regeneration.

results.result: JAK/STAT signaling is required for regeneration. Knockdown of upd1, upd2, Stat92E, or domeless using DUAL Control reduced regeneration, confirming pathway requirement in regenerating tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-71 are supported by wing scoring data (Figure 4—supplement 1E) showing significant reduction in regeneration upon knockdown of multiple JAK/STAT pathway components (p<0.0001 for most). The consistency across multiple pathway components strengthens the conclusion, though the effect of upd3 knockdown is less significant as expected given it lacks a damage-responsive peak.

results.result: CG9572/asperous (aspr) encodes a predicted secreted protein with sequence similarity to vertebrate Jagged, containing seven EGF-type repeats and a signal peptide but lacking a transmembrane domain or DSL domain. Tagged Aspr protein shows cytoplasmic and extracellular localization consistent with secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-76, C78-79 are supported by bioinformatic analysis (Figure 5—supplement 1A-D) showing sequence similarity to Jagged and domain predictions, and by immunofluorescence of tagged protein (Figures 5B-D) showing cytoplasmic localization and punctae in non-expressing cells consistent with secretion. The characterization is thorough and well-documented.

results.result: Aspr is expressed at low levels in undamaged discs but is strongly upregulated in the blastema following damage in early L3, with much weaker expression in late L3. Aspr knockdown delays Cut expression at the wing margin and weakly reduces Notch reporter activity, suggesting aspr may promote Notch signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-87 are supported by in situ hybridization (Figures 5E-J), MiMIC reporter analysis (Figures 5K-N), and genetic experiments showing delayed Cut expression and reduced NRE-GFP upon aspr knockdown (Figures 5O-S). However, the connection to Notch signaling is tentative as the effects are weak and the mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Aspr promotes regeneration. RNAi knockdown of aspr using DUAL Control and hemizygous aspr mutants both show strongly decreased regeneration, while overexpression does not improve regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C88-90 are supported by wing scoring data showing reduced regeneration with two different RNAi lines and a mutant allele (Figure 5V, p<0.0001), semi-quantitative PCR confirming the MiMIC line is a transcriptional mutant (Figure 5—supplement 2F), and overexpression data (Figure 5—supplement 2H). The consistency across multiple genetic manipulations strongly supports aspr's requirement for regeneration.

results.result: The apt gene shows the strongest DRMS chromatin accessibility signature in the ATAC-seq dataset. Apt encodes a b-Zip transcription factor known to restrict JAK/STAT signaling in the germline. Apt protein is expressed in peripodial epithelium and can be detected in the disc proper following damage in early L3 but not late L3.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-96 are supported by ATAC-seq data (Figures 2D, 6A), validated DRMS enhancer activity (Figure 2G-G'), citations to prior characterization of apt function (C93-94), and immunofluorescence showing stage-specific damage-induced expression (Figures 6B-C, Figure 6—supplement 1A-B). The characterization appropriately integrates new data with prior knowledge.

results.result: Apt curtails regeneration. Knockdown of apt using DUAL Control in both early and late L3 discs results in more complete adult wings compared to controls, with similar levels of cell death, suggesting apt normally limits regeneration. This is corroborated by hypomorphic apt mutants and correlates with increased STAT reporter activity in blastema cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C97-101 are well-supported by wing scoring data showing improved regeneration upon apt knockdown at both stages (Figure 6D, p<0.0001), DCP1 staining showing similar cell death levels (Figures 6E-F), mutant analysis (Figure 6—supplement 1C-D), and STAT-GFP reporter data showing increased JAK/STAT activity (Figures 6E-H). The data consistently support apt as a negative regulator of regeneration.

results.result: Reducing Polycomb-mediated silencing by knocking down esc improves regeneration in both early and late L3 discs. This improvement correlates with increased activity of multiple DRMS enhancers (DRMSWnt, DRMSMmp1, DRMSaspr) and increased expression of wg and Mmp1.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C103-108 are supported by wing scoring data showing improved regeneration with esc RNAi (Figure 6I, p<0.0001) and esc mutants (Figure 6—supplement 2C), and by reporter assays showing increased DRMS enhancer activity and protein expression (Figures 6J-K, Figure 6—supplement 2D-G). The data demonstrate that reducing PcG-mediated silencing can overcome suppression of regeneration by reactivating multiple DRMS enhancers simultaneously.

results.result: Prior work established that wg and Wnt6 are regulated by the BRV118 DRMS enhancer containing damage-responsive (BRV-B) and maturity-silencing (BRV-C) modules. BRV-B contains essential AP-1 binding sites, while BRV-C promotes Polycomb-mediated silencing. Restoring wg expression alone is insufficient to restore regeneration in mature discs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C16-22, C109-110 accurately summarize prior work (Harris et al., 2016) that is foundational to the current study. The claims are appropriately cited and the key finding that restoring wg alone is insufficient (C19, C110) motivates the search for additional DRMS enhancers in the current work.

results.result: The overall effect of multiple genes regulated by DRMS enhancers is likely to promote regeneration, as manipulation of the chromatin silencing factor esc can de-repress multiple DRMS enhancers and improve regeneration. However, the number of DRMS regions identified is likely an underestimate due to whole-disc analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-112, C128 represent reasonable inferences from the data. The conclusion that multiple DRMS-regulated genes collectively promote regeneration (C111) is supported by the esc knockdown experiments showing simultaneous de-repression of multiple enhancers and improved regeneration. The caveat about underestimation (C112) is appropriately acknowledged and justified by the experimental design limitations.

results.result: Aspr has sequence similarity to vertebrate Jagged but lacks key features of canonical Notch ligands (DSL domain, transmembrane domain). Aspr knockdown delays Cut and Notch reporter expression, suggesting it may promote Notch signaling, but overexpression does not increase Notch signaling. The role of Aspr in regeneration may be independent of direct Notch regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-122 present data and speculation about Aspr's relationship to Notch signaling. While the sequence similarity (C115) and effects on Cut/NRE-GFP (C114) are documented, the mechanistic connection to Notch signaling remains unclear. The lack of effect from overexpression (C121) and the incompatibility with canonical Notch activation mechanisms (C118-119) suggest the relationship is more complex than initially hypothesized. The conclusion that Aspr's role may be independent of Notch (C122) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Apt knockdown improves regeneration and increases STAT reporter expression, suggesting improvement might occur via increased JAK/STAT signaling. However, prior work showed that reducing JAK/STAT signaling reduced tissue loss without compromising proliferation, and overexpression of upd1/upd2 did not improve regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-126, C102 present data on apt's relationship to JAK/STAT signaling but the mechanism remains unclear. While apt knockdown increases STAT reporter activity (C101, C124), the relationship to regeneration is complicated by prior findings (C125-126) showing complex effects of JAK/STAT manipulation. The hypothesis that apt affects regeneration via JAK/STAT (C102, C124) is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: Reducing esc activity de-repressed multiple DRMS enhancers. The authors propose that an enhancer-mediated mechanism reducing expression of multiple genes may be more robust than single-regulator mechanisms, and that regeneration could be restored by either alleviating DRMS silencing or activating downstream pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-133 combine experimental findings (C127 supported by Figures 6J-K) with reasonable speculation about mechanisms (C128, C131-133). The parallel to prior work on cell cycle regulation (C129-130) is appropriately cited. The proposed mechanisms for restoring regeneration (C133) are logical extensions of the data, though they remain to be fully tested.

results.result: Loss of regenerative capacity with maturity is observed across diverse organisms including amphibians, mammals, and invertebrates. Damage-responsive enhancers have been identified in multiple species including zebrafish and mice, with evidence for conservation in humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-11, C135-140 appropriately cite and summarize prior work establishing the generality of age-dependent loss of regeneration across taxa and the existence of damage-responsive enhancers in other species. The citations appear accurate and the claims provide important context for the current work. The observation that it's unknown whether these enhancers become silenced with maturity in other species (C138) appropriately identifies a gap in knowledge.

results.result: Prior work has shown genome-wide chromatin changes during regeneration, the importance of Wnt signaling in regeneration across organisms, and that JAK/STAT can promote plasticity during regeneration. The study of damage-responsive enhancers could provide insights for human regenerative medicine.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-15, C134, C141 appropriately cite prior work providing context for the current study. The speculation about future implications for human medicine (C141) is reasonable given the evidence for conserved damage-responsive elements in humans (C140), though it remains speculative.

results.result: Ablation with egr using DUAL Control resulted in weaker adult phenotypes and lower levels of activated caspase compared to rpr ablation.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is supported by data in Figure 3—supplement 2A-E showing weaker wing phenotypes and reduced DCP1 staining with egr compared to rpr. This technical observation explains why rpr was chosen for subsequent wing scoring assays.
